title: Designing an AI feature people can trust
metaTitle: Trustworthy AI UX: source, limit, edit
excerpt: People trust an AI feature when they can see the source, the limit, and an easy edit. A confident wrong answer, with none of those, is a defect.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. Two people checking a screen together is the posture of verifying a source before trusting a result.
caption: Check the screen before trusting what it produced. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes an AI feature feel trustworthy?
faqs.answer: Show the source the result used, state the limit of what it considered, and land the result in a field the person can edit or discard. A confident answer with none of those is a defect, even when the prose is fluent. If there is no source, do not generate a factual claim.

faqs.question: Where should the limit be written?
faqs.answer: Write it in text beside the result, not only on a policy page or in a tooltip. Name what the feature did not see, such as mail that was never pasted in. A generic warning that mistakes are possible does not tell the person where to look.

faqs.question: Should the feature send or publish on its own?
faqs.answer: Leave sending, publishing, and charging until the person edits and takes an explicit action. Discard should be as available as accept, and earlier writing should stay recoverable. Anything a customer will see, pay, or be unable to undo still needs a person, even when the source is shown.

markdown:
Trustworthy AI UX is mostly three visible things: the source of the answer, the limit of what the feature will do, and an easy way to edit or discard the result. A confident wrong answer, with none of those, is a product defect. People do not experience it as a small miss. They experience it as the product lying.

Trust is not a tone. A warmer sentence does not repair a result the person cannot check. Show the basis, say what was not considered, and leave the person in control of what ships.

## Show the source

If the feature summarizes, drafts, or recommends, the person should be able to see what it used. A document, a record, a selection they highlighted, a catalog field. Name it in the interface, next to the result, in words a founder would accept on a customer call.

"Based on the last three project updates" is a source. "Here is a summary" is not. When the source is missing, the person has to trust the model or ignore the feature. Most people will ignore it after the first surprise, and the careful ones will check every line, which means the feature saved no time.

Keep the source close enough to open. A footnote that points at a system the person cannot access is decoration. A link, a quoted line, or the highlighted passage they already selected is something they can verify in the moment. Verification is the feature. The generated text is the convenience on top of it.

If there is no source, do not generate a factual claim. Offer a template, or ask for the fact. A product that fills a price, a date, or a promise from nothing will eventually fill in the wrong one, and it will look as sure as the right ones.

Put the source in the same visual hierarchy as the result. A pale caption under a bold paragraph will be skipped, and then the source may as well be absent. If the result is a paragraph, the first line can name the material. If the result is a list, each row can name the field it came from. People check what they can see without hunting.

## State the limit in the interface

Write the limit where the result appears, not in a policy page. One sentence is enough. This draft uses the selected notes and does not know about emails that were never pasted in. This recommendation covers the catalog fields and does not know about stock in the back room.

Limits change what the person does next. A stated limit invites a check. A hidden limit invites blame when the check fails in front of a customer. The copy can be calm. It should be specific. "AI can make mistakes" is true and useless. "This does not see refunds" tells the person where to look.

The W3C notes that the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) apply to AI web interfaces, organized under principles that include perceivable, operable, and understandable. A limit that is only a tooltip, or only a color, is easy to miss. Put it in text, in the same region as the result, so it can be read and reached.

## Make the edit the default

The result should land in a field the person was already going to review. A draft in the reply box. A suggested title in the title field. A list of changes they can accept one by one. The next action is editing, which is a familiar job.

A modal that says "Apply" and "Cancel," with the result already committed in spirit, pushes the person to accept. Prefer a state where nothing is sent, published, or charged until they say so. Discard has to be as obvious as accept. If discard is a small text button and accept is the only real control, the interface has chosen for them.

Leave their previous work intact. Replacing a paragraph they wrote, with no way back, teaches people not to use the feature on anything they care about. That is the opposite of trust. Version the text, or insert beside their draft, and let them take the sentences they want.

An example, labeled as an exercise: a support tool drafts a reply from the last three tickets and the refund policy. The draft sits in the composer. Above it, a line names those sources and says the draft cannot see the shipping carrier. The agent edits the date, deletes a sentence, and sends. If the sources were empty, the tool would have offered the policy link and left the composer blank.

## Confident and wrong is a defect

Treat a wrong factual answer as a bug, even if the prose was fluent. File it with the source that was missing or misread. Fix the retrieval, the prompt's boundary, or the decision to generate at all. Do not "tune the personality" and ship the same hole.

Measure the defect the way you measure a broken button. How often does a person substantially rewrite or discard the result. How often does a wrong claim leave the building. If discard is the common path, the feature is not ready, and hiding it behind a friendlier label will not make it ready.

Hanabi's standard on a product interface is clarity over complexity. An AI feature that is clear about source, limit, and edit is smaller than a chat that claims to know the business. Smaller is the point. The person still has the judgment. The feature did the gathering.

## Where a person still has to look

Some results should not be sendable on the model's word alone. Anything a customer will see, pay, or be unable to undo needs a human review, even when the source is shown. The line for that review is the next piece: [where a human still has to review the work](/blog/human-review-in-automation).

Show the source anyway. Review is faster when the person can see the basis, and it is honest when the limit is on the screen.
